questions.prompt:
A quality-control lab separates a volatile mixture of propanone, 1-propanol, and hexane by GC. Helium is the mobile phase and the stationary liquid coating is polar.

(a) Complete the comparison: for each analyte, identify its strongest IMF with itself and its expected affinity for the stationary phase.
(b) Rank the analytes from smallest to largest retention factor k. Explain the ranking as a competition between analyte–stationary and analyte–mobile interactions.

visual.title: Analytes and polar GC setup
visual.caption: Helium carries the vaporized analytes through the column.

hints: Decide whether each molecule can donate a hydrogen bond to itself before ranking its polarity.
Greater attraction to the stationary phase gives larger k.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.1 Identify the IMFs that hold multiple copies of molecules together

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.5c Gas chromatography (GC)

questions.answer: Propanone is polar and its strongest IMF with itself is dipole–dipole (plus London); it has appreciable affinity for a polar coating. 1-Propanol has hydrogen bonding with itself and strongest affinity for the polar coating. Hexane has London dispersion only and the weakest polar-coating affinity. Smallest to largest k: hexane < propanone < 1-propanol. Strong stationary-phase attraction holds an analyte longer; helium is inert/nonpolar and chiefly carries analytes forward.
rubric: Identifies London-only hexane, dipole–dipole propanone, and hydrogen-bonding 1-propanol.
Relates each analyte’s polarity/IMF to a polar stationary phase.
Ranks k as hexane < propanone < 1-propanol.
Explains that stronger stationary-phase attraction gives greater retention.
questions.explanation: The analysis is a phase-affinity comparison, not a memorized peak order.

questions.prompt:
Three separate beakers contain (i) NaCl in water, (ii) iodine, I₂, near water, and (iii) ethanol mixed with water.

(a) Name the most important attraction between the species named in each beaker.
(b) For NaCl in water, draw the orientation of one water molecule around Na⁺ and around Cl⁻. Explain why the two orientations must differ.

visual.title: Water approaching dissolved ions
visual.caption: Draw the partial-charge ends of water in your response.

hints: An ion interacting with a polar molecule is a distinct category from a hydrogen bond.
Water has a δ− oxygen end and δ+ hydrogen ends.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.1 Identify the IMFs that hold multiple copies of molecules together

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.4 Impact of IMFs on solubility

questions.answer: NaCl in water: ion–dipole. I₂ near water: dipole–induced dipole, because polar water can induce a temporary dipole in nonpolar I₂. Ethanol + water: hydrogen bonding. Around Na⁺, water’s δ− oxygen faces the cation; around Cl⁻, water’s δ+ hydrogen end faces the anion. Opposite ion charges attract opposite partial ends of water.
rubric: Names ion–dipole, dipole–induced dipole, and hydrogen bonding for the three beakers.
Orients water oxygen toward Na⁺.
Orients water hydrogen end toward Cl⁻.
Explains the opposite orientations with electrostatic attraction.
questions.explanation: The inducer can be a permanent dipole as well as an ion.

questions.prompt:
A student labels every molecule that contains O, N, or F as “hydrogen bonding.” Consider CH₃F, CH₃OCH₃, and CH₃CH₂OH.

(a) For each pure substance, identify the strongest IMF it forms with itself.
(b) Which of the three can accept a hydrogen bond from water, and which can donate one to water? Explain why the answers are not identical.

visual.title: Bonding clues
visual.caption: Use the actual covalent bond to the hydrogen, not merely the presence of an electronegative atom.

hints: A molecule can have a suitable lone pair but no suitable donor H.
All molecular substances also have London dispersion.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.1 Identify the IMFs that hold multiple copies of molecules together

questions.answer: CH₃F: dipole–dipole (plus London), not self hydrogen bonding. CH₃OCH₃: dipole–dipole (plus London), not self hydrogen bonding. CH₃CH₂OH: hydrogen bonding. All three can accept a hydrogen bond from water: F and O have lone pairs. Only ethanol can donate a hydrogen bond because it has H directly bonded to O. Neither a C–H nor the mere presence of F/O creates a donor.
rubric: Does not falsely assign self hydrogen bonding to CH₃F or dimethyl ether.
Assigns ethanol hydrogen bonding.
Correctly identifies all three as water H-bond acceptors under this course treatment.
Identifies only ethanol as a donor and explains the direct O–H requirement.
questions.explanation: Donor and acceptor conditions are separate; a lone pair alone does not make a molecule self-hydrogen-bonding.

questions.prompt:
The data below are for pure substances.

(a) Rank them from lowest to highest boiling point and explain your reasoning using both force type and molecular size.
(b) Explain why it would be wrong to use only the statement “dipole–dipole is stronger than London dispersion” to rank HCl and octane.

visual.title: Substances to compare
visual.caption: Use the information in the table together with IMF reasoning.

hints: For similar size, IMF type is a strong guide; this set is not all similar size.
More electrons and more surface area increase total London attraction.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.3 Rank IMFs by strength

questions.answer: Lowest to highest boiling point: methane < HCl < NH₃ < octane. CH₄ has only very weak London forces. HCl adds dipole–dipole. NH₃ hydrogen-bonds. Octane is nonpolar, but its many electrons and large surface give enough summed London dispersion to exceed the small polar molecules. “Dipole–dipole is stronger per comparable contact” cannot settle HCl versus octane because the substances differ drastically in size and polarizability.
rubric: Ranks CH₄ < HCl < NH₃ < octane.
Uses force type for the small molecules.
Uses octane’s size/electrons/surface area for its strong total London forces.
Explains why force rankings require comparable molecular size.
questions.explanation: London forces are weakest per interaction but can dominate when there are many contacts.

questions.prompt:
n-Pentane, 2-methylbutane, and neopentane all have formula C₅H₁₂.

(a) Rank their boiling points from lowest to highest.
(b) Explain why formula, molar mass, and dominant IMF are not enough to make them tie. Your explanation must refer to a molecular shape feature and the number/quality of contacts between molecules.

visual.title: Three C₅H₁₂ carbon skeletons
visual.caption: All three have London dispersion as their dominant IMF.

hints: Straight molecules can touch neighboring molecules along more surface.
Do not invent a dipole or hydrogen bonding in these hydrocarbons.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.3 Rank IMFs by strength

questions.answer: Lowest to highest boiling point: neopentane < 2-methylbutane < n-pentane. All are nonpolar and rely on London dispersion, but the long straight n-pentane molecules have the greatest contact surface and strongest summed attractions. More branching makes molecules compact and reduces effective surface contact; neopentane is most compact.
rubric: Ranks neopentane < 2-methylbutane < n-pentane.
States that all share London dispersion and the same formula/mass.
Explains the ranking through surface area/contact and branching.
questions.explanation: Shape changes total dispersion contact without changing the molecular formula.

questions.prompt:
A GC column has a polar stationary phase. An unretained methane marker appears first at 1.5 min. The mixture’s two analyte peaks appear at 3.0 min and 7.5 min.

(a) Calculate k for both analyte peaks.
(b) The analytes are pentane and 1-propanol. Assign each analyte to a peak and explain the IMF-based reason.
(c) State what the first peak represents and why it is not helium.

visual.title: GC output
visual.caption: The first peak is from the methane marker introduced with the sample.

hints: Use the first peak’s time as tₘ.
A later peak means stronger interaction with the stationary phase.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.5b Reading a chromatogram: t_R, t_m, and k

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.5c Gas chromatography (GC)

questions.answer: For 3.0 min, k=(3.0−1.5)/1.5=1.0. For 7.5 min, k=(7.5−1.5)/1.5=4.0. Pentane is the 3.0-min peak because it is nonpolar and has weak attraction to the polar stationary phase. 1-Propanol is the 7.5-min peak because its polar O–H group gives strong interactions, including hydrogen bonding, with the polar phase. The 1.5-min peak is the methane void-time marker, not helium; helium flows continuously and is the baseline/mobile phase.
rubric: Calculates k = 1.0 and k = 4.0.
Assigns pentane earlier and 1-propanol later based on polar-phase affinity.
Identifies methane as the void marker.
Explains why continuous helium is not a chromatogram peak.
questions.explanation: Retention factor reports time retained relative to time moving with the mobile phase.

questions.prompt:
Pentane and 1-propanol are instead separated by reverse-phase HPLC with a nonpolar stationary phase and a methanol/water mobile phase.

(a) Rank the two analytes from earliest to latest elution and explain the tug of war with both phases.
(b) If 1-propanol is taking too long to elute, state the specified change to the mobile-phase composition and why it decreases tR.

visual.title: Reverse-phase HPLC setup
visual.caption: Use the phase properties to determine which interactions dominate.

hints: Ask which analyte is carried especially well by the mobile liquid.
The course notes specify how increasing the water fraction changes the mobile phase.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.5d High performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), reverse phase

questions.answer: Earliest to latest: 1-propanol < pentane. 1-Propanol interacts strongly with polar methanol/water and less with the nonpolar stationary phase, so it is carried through faster. Pentane has London compatibility with the nonpolar stationary phase and is retained longer. To decrease 1-propanol’s tR, increase the water fraction; this makes the mobile phase more polar and strengthens the analyte–mobile interaction.
rubric: Ranks 1-propanol before pentane.
Uses both the nonpolar stationary phase and polar mobile phase to justify the result.
Increases water fraction and correctly connects it to lower tR.
questions.explanation: Reverse phase flips the GC retention logic because the stationary phase’s polarity flips.

questions.prompt:
Predict whether each pair forms a well-mixed solution or separates into layers: ethanol + water, octanol + water, and hexane + water.

(a) Complete the prediction for all three.
(b) For octanol + water, explain why the molecule’s O–H group does not automatically make the whole molecule highly water-soluble.
(c) Explain what water–water attractions would have to be replaced if hexane mixed with water.

visual.title: Solvent-pair evidence
visual.caption: Judge the balance of the whole molecule, not just one functional group.

hints: As an alcohol’s hydrocarbon tail grows, its water solubility falls.
Mixing must replace attractions already present in both pure liquids.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.4 Impact of IMFs on solubility

questions.answer: Ethanol + water mixes well; octanol + water has low solubility and tends to separate; hexane + water separates. Octanol’s one O–H can hydrogen-bond, but its long eight-carbon nonpolar tail dominates the molecule’s interactions and becomes increasingly unfavorable in water. For hexane to mix, water would give up strong water–water hydrogen bonds and replace them chiefly with weak London contacts to hexane, which is unfavorable.
rubric: Correctly predicts ethanol/water mixing and poor mixing for octanol/water and hexane/water.
Explains the long nonpolar octanol tail outweighing one OH group.
Identifies water–water hydrogen bonds and weak hexane contacts as the unfavorable replacement.
questions.explanation: Solubility depends on whether new solute–solvent attractions can replace the attractions broken in the pure substances.

questions.prompt:
A student claims that boiling a beaker of water breaks the O–H covalent bonds, leaving hydrogen and oxygen atoms in the vapor.

(a) Correct the claim by identifying what attractions are disrupted during boiling and what chemical formula the vapor still has.
(b) Compare an intramolecular covalent bond and an intermolecular force in terms of where it acts and which process normally disrupts it.
hints: Steam is not a new substance.
Use the words within and between carefully.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.2 How IMFs differ from covalent bonds

questions.answer: Boiling water disrupts hydrogen bonds and other intermolecular attractions between separate H₂O molecules; the vapor is still H₂O. A covalent O–H bond is within one molecule and shares electrons; an IMF is between separate molecules. Phase changes and dissolving normally disrupt IMFs, while chemical reactions are needed to break/rearrange covalent bonds.
rubric: States that steam remains H₂O.
Identifies intermolecular hydrogen bonds, not O–H bonds, as disrupted by boiling.
Distinguishes within-molecule covalent bonds from between-molecule IMFs.
Links phase change to IMF disruption and reaction to covalent change.
questions.explanation: A change of state does not normally change a substance’s chemical identity.

questions.prompt:
At about 288 K, Earth has liquid water and methane is a gas. At about 94 K on Titan, methane forms liquid lakes and water is solid ice.

(a) Complete a two-column explanation by identifying the dominant IMF for each substance.
(b) Explain all four phase observations using the competition between thermal energy and intermolecular attraction.
(c) State why “methane is a gas” is not a complete chemical property statement.

visual.title: Planetary conditions
visual.caption: Compare the molecules’ attractions with the thermal energy available at each location.

hints: Water and methane do not have the same strongest interaction.
A lower temperature changes molecular kinetic energy.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.6 IMFs vs thermal energy: why phases differ (Lecture 10, Titan)

questions.answer: Water’s dominant IMF is a hydrogen-bond network; methane’s is London dispersion. At warm Earth conditions, water’s strong network can still maintain a liquid while methane’s weak London forces lose to greater thermal motion and methane is gaseous. At cold Titan conditions, thermal energy is so low that methane’s weak London forces can condense it, while water’s strong hydrogen bonds dominate and water is solid. “Methane is a gas” is incomplete because phase depends on temperature/thermal energy as well as attraction strength.
rubric: Identifies water hydrogen bonding and methane London dispersion.
Explains Earth and Titan outcomes using different available thermal energy.
Explains methane condensation at low temperature despite weak IMFs.
Rejects an intrinsic, temperature-free phase label.
questions.explanation: Phase is the outcome of intermolecular attractions competing with molecular kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: The highest-mass peaks for an unknown are shown. (a) State what the spacing and relative heights say about the atom(s) in the intact molecule. (b) A lower-mass pair occurs at m/z 63 and 65 in about a 3:1 ratio. Explain what the lower pair says about the charged fragment and why the neutral piece from its formation is absent from the spectrum.

visual.title: Highest-mass region
visual.caption: This is the highest-mass cluster observed.

hints: Compare the pattern with the one-atom and two-atom isotope patterns in your table.
A charged fragment retains any isotope signature from atoms that remain in it.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 1.5 Interpret mass spectra to determine the mass and chemical formula of a substance

questions.answer: The 128:130 pair is M:M+2 ≈ 3:2, which is the two-chlorine pattern (approximately 9:6:1; the M+4 member may be too small to show here). The 63:65 pair at 3:1 means the charged fragment retains one Cl. The complementary neutral fragment is not detected because the instrument detects ions, not neutral radicals or molecules.
rubric: Recognizes a two-Cl isotope cluster rather than a one-Cl or one-Br pattern.
Identifies one Cl retained in the 63/65 charged fragment from its 3:1 pair.
States that neutral products are invisible to the detector.
questions.explanation: Chlorine isotope patterns remain attached to any ion that still contains chlorine.

questions.prompt: A molecule has two chlorine atoms. Use 0.75 for the fraction of ³⁵Cl and 0.25 for the fraction of ³⁷Cl. (a) Calculate the probabilities for the all-light, mixed, and all-heavy chlorine combinations. (b) Give the resulting M : M+2 : M+4 ratio and explain why the mixed term must include a factor of 2.
hints: There are two distinguishable ways to get one light and one heavy isotope.
Normalize the three probabilities to the smallest one for a simple ratio.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 1.9 Predict simple fragmentation patterns for hydrocarbons and halogenated hydrocarbons

questions.answer: P(³⁵Cl–³⁵Cl) = 0.75² = 0.5625. P(mixed) = 2(0.75)(0.25) = 0.375. P(³⁷Cl–³⁷Cl) = 0.25² = 0.0625. Dividing by 0.0625 gives 9:6:1. The mixed outcome has ³⁵Cl on either of the two chlorine positions, so both arrangements count.
rubric: Gives 9:6:1 for M:M+2:M+4.
Explains the factor of 2 as the two mixed arrangements.
questions.explanation: Forgetting the two mixed arrangements is the usual source of the wrong middle peak.

questions.prompt: For HCN, (a) use the HAVE/NEED method to determine the total number of bonds and lone pairs, then draw a Lewis structure. (b) Calculate the formal charge on each atom and decide whether the molecule has a net molecular dipole. Give the geometry about carbon as part of your reasoning.
hints: Hydrogen needs 2 electrons; C and N each need 8.
For formal charge, count lone-pair electrons rather than lone-pair pairs.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 1.6 Draw and evaluate Lewis structures

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 2.9 Use VSEPR to predict shape and polarity

questions.answer: HAVE = 1 + 4 + 5 = 10 e⁻. NEED = 2 + 8 + 8 = 18 e⁻. Bonding electrons = 8, so there are 4 bonds; lone-pair electrons = 2, so there is one lone pair. The structure is H–C≡N: with the lone pair on N. FC(H)=0, FC(C)=0, FC(N)=0. Carbon has two domains and is linear. The C–H and C≡N bond dipoles do not cancel because the ends differ, so HCN is polar.
rubric: Obtains 10 HAVE electrons, 18 NEED electrons, four bonds, and one lone pair.
Draws H–C≡N with the lone pair on N.
Gets zero formal charge on all three atoms.
Uses linear geometry and unequal ends to justify a net dipole.
questions.explanation: A linear molecule is nonpolar only when its opposing dipoles are equal and opposite.

questions.prompt: Electron ionization of a hydrocarbon produces intense ions at m/z 15, 29, 43, and 57, separated by 14 mass units. (a) Assign a chemically plausible formula to the m/z 43 ion. (b) Explain which family of bonds is preferentially breaking and use the bond-energy trend to explain why this is more likely than loss of hydrogen atoms.
hints: A 14-unit difference is one CH₂ group.
Compare the course-average strengths of C–C and C–H bonds.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 1.9 Predict simple fragmentation patterns for hydrocarbons and halogenated hydrocarbons

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 1.8 Define bond dissociation energies and use them to evaluate bond strength

questions.answer: m/z 43 can be C₃H₇⁺. The repeated 14-unit spacing is the alkyl-cation sequence, so C–C cleavage is common. C–C bonds are about 348 kJ/mol while C–H bonds are about 413 kJ/mol; weaker C–C bonds are easier to break, whereas simple H loss is comparatively rare.
rubric: Assigns a plausible alkyl cation such as C₃H₇⁺ to m/z 43.
Connects 14-unit spacing to CH₂/alkyl fragments.
Uses the lower C–C BDE to justify preferential C–C cleavage.
questions.explanation: The base peak reports the most abundant ion, not necessarily the intact molecule.

questions.prompt: A student says: “IR sends radio waves into a sample, and an upward feature means the sample absorbed more light.” (a) Correct both errors, including what must match for absorption to occur. (b) On the supplied sketch, explain why the curve is much steeper when the nuclei are pushed too close together than when the bond is stretched toward dissociation.

visual.title: Bond potential-energy sketch
visual.caption: The nodes mark positions along a potential-energy curve, not energy levels.

hints: Separate the kind of electromagnetic radiation from the detector’s vertical axis.
Think about repulsion at very short internuclear distance.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 2.2 Explain absorption spectroscopy

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 2.3 Illustrate with potential energy diagrams how light excites vibrational energy levels

questions.answer: IR uses infrared light, not radio waves; radio waves are used for NMR. Absorption occurs when photon energy matches a quantized energy gap, E = hν = ΔE. In a transmittance spectrum, absorption removes light, so the plotted %T dips downward. Compression produces a steep rise because close nuclei strongly repel; stretching gradually weakens attraction until the curve reaches the separated-atom/dissociation plateau.
rubric: Correctly distinguishes IR from NMR radiation.
States the energy-matching condition for absorption.
Explains downward transmittance dips.
Explains short-distance nuclear repulsion and the dissociation plateau.
questions.explanation: The asymmetric well is physical: compression and dissociation have different energy behavior.

questions.prompt: For this question, assume a C–C single bond and a C–N single bond are both observable. (a) Calculate the reduced mass of each using C = 12 and N = 14. (b) Predict which one absorbs at the higher wavenumber if their force constants are comparable. (c) A C=C bond has a stretching signal at 1650 cm⁻¹. If the question explicitly tells you to assume force constant is proportional to bond order, estimate the C≡C stretching wavenumber.
hints: Reduced mass is a product divided by a sum, not the sum of the masses.
For the last part, wavenumber scales with the square root of the force constant.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 2.8 Correlate bond force constant and reduced mass to IR wavenumber

questions.answer: μred(C–C) = 12×12/(12+12) = 6.00. μred(C–N) = 12×14/(12+14) = 6.46. With comparable k, C–C has lower reduced mass and therefore higher wavenumber. If k(C≡C)=3⁄2 k(C=C), then ṽ(C≡C)=1650√1.5≈2020 cm⁻¹.
rubric: Uses product-over-sum and obtains 6.00 and about 6.46.
Chooses C–C as higher wavenumber under the stated comparable-k condition.
Uses square-root scaling and estimates about 2020 cm⁻¹.
questions.explanation: The bond-order scaling is only valid because the question explicitly supplied that approximation.

questions.prompt: An unknown has the absorptions represented below. (a) Identify the two most diagnostic bond features and give the most supported functional-group class. (b) Explain why the low-transmittance portions point downward, and state which side of a standard IR spectrum has higher wavenumber.

visual.title: IR observations
visual.caption: The trace is schematic; only the marked regions are intended as evidence.

hints: Use the combination of features, not one peak alone.
In transmittance mode, less light arriving at the detector means a lower plotted value.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 2.4 Explain the axes and data points on an IR spectrum

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 2.14 Interpret an IR spectrum to identify functional groups

questions.answer: A strong sharp absorption near 1715 cm⁻¹ indicates C=O and a strong feature near 1220 cm⁻¹ supports C–O. With no broad O–H feature, the best-supported class is an ester. Dips point down because the graph is % transmittance: more absorption means less transmitted light. Higher wavenumber is on the left of the standard 4000→400 cm⁻¹ axis.
rubric: Identifies C=O and C–O evidence.
Concludes ester and rules out an O–H-containing alternative using the absent broad feature.
Explains the transmittance dip and reverse x-axis direction.
questions.explanation: A combination of diagnostic signals is safer than identifying a whole molecule from one peak.

questions.prompt: Consider N₂, HCl, and the symmetric stretch of CO₂. (a) Predict which cases have an observable IR stretching absorption and justify each by what happens to the molecular dipole during the vibration. (b) Compare the expected intensity of C=O and C=C stretches in otherwise similar molecules, and explain the difference without claiming that every double bond is equally intense.
hints: Ask whether the vibration changes dipole moment, not simply whether a bond exists.
Intensity tracks the size of the dipole change.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 2.11 Explain how vibrational modes can be IR active or inactive

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 2.12 Predict the relative intensity of IR signals

questions.answer: N₂ is IR inactive because its stretch never creates a changing dipole. HCl is active because stretching changes its polar bond dipole. The symmetric stretch of CO₂ is inactive because the equal C=O dipoles change but remain cancelling. C=O is generally much more intense than C=C because its larger polarity produces a larger dipole change during stretching; symmetry can further weaken or eliminate a C=C response.
rubric: Correctly calls N₂ inactive, HCl active, and CO₂ symmetric stretch inactive.
Justifies each outcome using change in dipole moment.
Ranks C=O more intense than C=C and links it to polarity/dipole change.
questions.explanation: IR activity and IR intensity both depend on dipole behavior, but they answer different questions.

questions.prompt: For each central atom in SO₂, (a) state the electron geometry and molecular shape, then give the approximate bond angle. (b) Draw the two S–O bond dipoles and decide whether they cancel. Explain why “two equal bond dipoles” alone is not enough to decide the answer.

visual.title: SO₂ connectivity
visual.caption: Use electron domains around sulfur; this schematic is not drawn to an angle scale.

hints: A double bond is one electron domain for VSEPR.
Molecular shape ignores the lone pair, but the lone pair still changes the geometry.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 2.9 Use VSEPR to predict shape and polarity

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 2.10 Draw and identify the direction and relative magnitude of bond dipoles

questions.answer: SO₂ has three electron domains around S: two bonds and one lone pair, so its electron geometry is trigonal planar and its molecular shape is bent, with an angle slightly less than 120° (about 119°). Each dipole points S→O. In the bent arrangement the vectors do not oppose at 180°, so a net dipole remains. Equal magnitude alone does not guarantee cancellation; the directions/geometry must be symmetric.
rubric: States trigonal-planar electron geometry and bent molecular shape.
Gives an angle below 120° and attributes compression to the lone pair.
Draws dipoles toward O and concludes they do not cancel.
Distinguishes equal dipoles from vector cancellation.
questions.explanation: Lone pairs are omitted from the molecular-shape name but not from their geometric effect.

questions.prompt: Without using numerical BDE values, rank H–F, H–Cl, H–Br, and H–I from strongest to weakest. Then explain why both atom size and electronegativity support your order. Finally, state which bond has the larger electronegativity difference, H–F or H–Cl, and why that fact should not be used to calculate an exact BDE.
hints: Moving down a group changes both bond length and electronegativity.
Use electronegativity to reason about direction and relative ionic character, not as a direct BDE calculator.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 2.6 Predict relative bond strengths WITHOUT BDE values

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 2.5 Predict relative size, mass, and electronegativity from the periodic table

questions.answer: H–F > H–Cl > H–Br > H–I. Down the halogen group atoms become larger, making longer, weaker overlap with H. Electronegativity also falls down the group, so the partial-charge attraction/ionic character decreases. H–F has the larger Δχ (4.0−2.2=1.8 versus 3.2−2.2=1.0). Δχ supports ranking but is not proportional to BDE, so it cannot by itself give an exact bond energy.
rubric: Gives the correct strongest-to-weakest order.
Uses increasing size/bond length to explain weakening down the group.
Uses decreasing Δχ as a second supporting factor.
States H–F has larger Δχ and does not overclaim exact BDE prediction.
questions.explanation: The trend is strongest when multiple chemical principles point to the same conclusion.

questions.prompt: An unknown has formula C₄H₈O. (a) Calculate its degree of unsaturation. (b) Draw two constitutional isomers consistent with that result: one containing a C=O and one containing a C=C. For each, state one feature you would use to distinguish the two kinds of structures using an IR spectrum.
hints: Oxygen is omitted from the degree-of-unsaturation equation.
A degree of unsaturation can be a ring or one π bond.

sourceRefs.heading: 3.2 Calculate and interpret degrees of unsaturation (DoU)

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md

questions.answer: DoU = (2(4)+2−8)/2 = 1. One carbonyl isomer is butanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO; one alkene isomer is CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂OH (one of several valid alkene structures). The carbonyl compound has a strong, sharp C=O absorption around 1650–1750 cm⁻¹. The alkene has a C=C feature around 1600–1680 cm⁻¹ and may show =C–H just above 3000 cm⁻¹, but no carbonyl peak.
rubric: Calculates DoU = 1.
Draws valid constitutional isomers with a carbonyl versus C=C.
Uses the presence/absence of C=O and an appropriate alkene feature to distinguish them.

questions.prompt: A student draws CH₃CH₂CH₂OH once as a zigzag with the OH on the right, and again with the paper rotated so the OH appears on the left. (a) Decide whether the two drawings are constitutional isomers, the same compound, or neither. (b) Give a reliable procedure for deciding this in a harder case, then contrast it with 1-propanol versus 2-propanol.
hints: Track which atoms are connected to which; do not judge by the picture’s pose.
Constitutional isomers have the same formula but different connectivity.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 3.1 Define, identify and draw constitutional isomers

questions.answer: The rotated drawings of 1-propanol are the same compound: every atom has the same neighbors. In a harder case, write or trace the connectivity of each structure, then compare which atoms are bonded; do not use page orientation or a bent drawing as evidence. 1-propanol and 2-propanol are constitutional isomers because the OH-bearing carbon has different connectivity/position in the carbon chain.
rubric: Calls rotated 1-propanol the same compound.
Describes connectivity comparison as the decision method.
Correctly calls 1-propanol and 2-propanol constitutional isomers.
questions.explanation: A drawing can rotate or flip without changing a molecule; a constitutional isomer changes bonds between atoms.

questions.prompt: For CH₃CH₂Cl, (a) predict the number of distinct ¹H NMR signals and the integration ratio. (b) predict the splitting of each signal using hydrogens within three bonds. (c) decide which signal is farther downfield and explain the full induction-to-shielding reasoning chain.

visual.title: Two proton environments
visual.caption: Hydrogens attached to a displayed carbon belong to that environment.

hints: Equivalent H atoms give one signal; integration counts H, whereas splitting counts neighboring H.
An electronegative atom withdraws electron density through σ bonds.

questions.answer: CH₃CH₂Cl has two signals with 3:2 integration. The CH₃ signal is a triplet from two neighboring CH₂ H; the CH₂ signal is a quartet from three neighboring CH₃ H. CH₂Cl is farther downfield because Cl withdraws electron density inductively, leaving those H nuclei less shielded from the external field, so they resonate at higher frequency/higher ppm.
rubric: Gives two signals and 3:2 integration.
Gives CH₃ triplet and CH₂ quartet using all H within three bonds.
Places CH₂Cl downfield and explains induction → lower electron density → less shielding → higher ppm.
questions.explanation: Integration answers how many H are in an environment; splitting is a separate neighbor count.

(b) Explain how symmetry causes the ether result. (c) State one reason the two compounds could have the same molecular formula but still be distinguished using another spectroscopy method in this unit.

Same formula does not imply identical bond types.

questions.answer: Ethanol has three main environments under this course treatment: CH₃, CH₂, and OH. Dimethyl ether has one: its two CH₃ groups are related by symmetry, so all six H are equivalent. The two formulas are both C₂H₆O but their connectivity differs; IR can distinguish ethanol’s O–H broad absorption from ether’s lack of O–H (and both may show C–O).
rubric: Gives ethanol 3 signals and dimethyl ether 1.
Uses symmetry to make the ether methyl groups equivalent.
Uses an O–H IR feature to distinguish the compounds.
questions.explanation: MS alone has the same molecular mass for constitutional isomers; a bond-sensitive method helps.

(b) Explain both the single signal and the absence of splitting; be explicit about which hydrogens are or are not within three bonds. (c) Predict whether its mass spectrum would show an M:M+2 pair closer to 3:1 or 1:1.
hints: Nine equivalent H suggests three equivalent methyl groups.
A chlorine atom has a diagnostic two-isotope pattern.

questions.answer: The structure is tert-butyl chloride, (CH₃)₃C–Cl. Three equivalent CH₃ groups give one 9H environment. The adjacent central carbon has no hydrogens, so n = 0 and the methyl signal is a singlet. One chlorine gives an M:M+2 pattern near 3:1.

Explains the single 9H signal by equivalence of three methyl groups.
Explains singlet as no adjacent central-carbon H.
Selects the one-chlorine 3:1 isotope pattern.

questions.prompt: Consider pure NH₃ and PH₃. (a) Draw enough Lewis/VSEPR information to determine whether each molecule is polar. (b) Identify the strongest intermolecular force in each pure sample and decide which sample is held together more strongly. Your answer must distinguish a real hydrogen bond from an ordinary dipole interaction.
hints: Both central atoms have three bonds and one lone pair.
For this course, hydrogen bonding requires H directly bonded to N, O, or F.

questions.answer: Both NH₃ and PH₃ are trigonal pyramidal and polar because each has three bonds plus one lone pair. NH₃ has hydrogen bonding, since H is directly bonded to N; PH₃ does not meet the N/O/F requirement and is held mainly by weaker dipole–dipole and London interactions. NH₃ is held together more strongly.
rubric: States trigonal pyramidal/polar for both.
Identifies NH₃ hydrogen bonding.
Does not incorrectly assign hydrogen bonding to PH₃.
Concludes NH₃ has stronger IMFs.
questions.explanation: A polar molecule need not hydrogen-bond; the atom bonded to H matters.

questions.prompt: Rank CH₄, CH₃OCH₃, CH₃CH₂OH, and H₂O from lowest to highest boiling point. Then compare n-pentane with neopentane: they have the same formula and London forces only, so explain why their boiling points can still differ.
hints: First identify the strongest interaction available between copies of each molecule.
London dispersion depends on polarizability and contact surface, not just formula.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.3 Rank IMFs by strength

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.4 Impact of IMFs on solubility

questions.answer: CH₄ < CH₃OCH₃ < CH₃CH₂OH < H₂O. Methane has only weak London forces; ether has dipole–dipole; ethanol hydrogen-bonds; water forms an especially extensive hydrogen-bond network. n-Pentane has a larger contact surface than compact neopentane, so its London dispersion interactions are stronger and its boiling point is higher.
rubric: Gives the correct four-compound order.
Identifies the relevant IMF progression.
Explains n-pentane/neopentane using surface contact and London forces.
questions.explanation: Molecular shape changes how much temporary-dipole contact molecules can make.

questions.prompt: A gas-chromatography run has a polar liquid stationary phase and helium carrier gas. Hexane and 1-butanol are injected. (a) Assign the analytes to the later and earlier peaks. (b) The first peak at 1.2 min is a methane marker; later peaks occur at 4.0 and 7.6 min. Calculate k for each later peak and state what a larger k means physically.

visual.title: Chromatogram
visual.caption: The 1.2-min methane marker defines the void time.

hints: Like interacts with like: compare each analyte to the polar stationary coating.
Use k = (tR − tm)/tm, with methane as tm.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md

questions.answer: Hexane elutes earlier in polar-phase GC; 1-butanol interacts strongly with the polar stationary phase, including hydrogen bonding, and elutes later. For 4.0 min, k=(4.0−1.2)/1.2=2.33. For 7.6 min, k=(7.6−1.2)/1.2=5.33. The larger k means the analyte spends more time retained in the stationary phase relative to mobile-phase travel.
rubric: Assigns hexane earlier and 1-butanol later in polar GC.
Calculates k = 2.33 and 5.33.
Interprets larger k as greater stationary-phase retention.
questions.explanation: The methane peak is the void-time marker, not a helium peak.

questions.prompt: The same two analytes from Question 8 are now run by reverse-phase HPLC with a nonpolar stationary phase and methanol/water mobile phase. (a) Predict which elutes first and rationalize using the phases, not a memorized order. (b) A polar analyte is retained too long. State one change to the mobile phase that decreases tR and explain why.
hints: Ask which phase each analyte interacts with more strongly.
In this course setup, increasing water makes the mobile phase more polar.

sourceRefs.heading: 4.5d High performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), reverse phase

questions.answer: In reverse-phase HPLC, 1-butanol elutes first because it is more polar, interacts well with the polar methanol/water mobile phase, and is less retained by the nonpolar stationary phase. Hexane is retained longer by the nonpolar stationary phase. To shorten a polar analyte’s tR, increase the water fraction: the more polar mobile phase carries the polar analyte more strongly.
rubric: Assigns polar 1-butanol first in reverse phase.
Uses the polarity of both phases to justify the order.
Increases water fraction and correctly connects it to lower retention.
questions.explanation: The order flips because the stationary phase changes from polar GC coating to nonpolar reverse-phase HPLC material.

questions.prompt: Water is liquid on Earth near 288 K, while methane is liquid on Titan near 94 K; water there is solid. Explain the outcomes by (a) identifying the dominant intermolecular forces for H₂O and CH₄ and (b) comparing those forces with thermal energy at each location. Do not answer as though “gas” or “liquid” is an intrinsic property of a substance.
hints: Name the IMF, then explicitly discuss available thermal energy.
A lower temperature can let even weak attractions condense a substance.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 4.6 IMFs vs thermal energy: why phases differ (Lecture 10, Titan)

questions.answer: H₂O has a strong hydrogen-bond network; CH₄ has only weak London dispersion. At Earth’s higher temperature, methane’s weak attractions lose to thermal motion and methane is gaseous, while water’s strong network can sustain a liquid. At Titan’s much lower temperature, even methane’s weak London forces can condense it, while water’s much stronger interactions dominate enough to make solid ice. Phase depends on IMF strength relative to thermal energy, not a permanent label.
rubric: Identifies hydrogen bonding for water and London forces for methane.
Relates Earth’s and Titan’s temperatures to molecular kinetic/thermal energy.
Explains all stated phases as an IMF-versus-thermal-energy competition.
questions.explanation: The same molecule can occupy different phases at different temperatures.

questions.prompt: For each species, identify whether it is neutral or charged and whether it has an unpaired electron: Na⁺, NH₄⁺, Cl•, and [M]•⁺ formed when a molecule loses one electron in mass spectrometry. Then state the precise difference between an isotope pair and an ion pair of the same element.
hints: Charge comes from unequal numbers of protons and electrons; a dot has a distinct meaning.
An isotope keeps the same atomic number.

questions.answer: Na⁺ is charged but has no unpaired electron in its closed-shell ion. NH₄⁺ is charged and has no unpaired electron. Cl• is neutral and has one unpaired electron. [M]•⁺ is charged and has an unpaired electron: loss of one electron makes a radical cation. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers/masses. Ions differ in electron number and therefore charge.
rubric: Classifies charge and radical status for all four species.
Defines [M]•⁺ as a radical cation formed by electron loss.
Distinguishes isotope neutron/mass change from ion electron/charge change.
questions.explanation: The dot means an unpaired electron, not merely an electrical charge.

questions.prompt: Chlorine has isotope masses 34.969 and 36.966. Its average atomic mass is 35.45. (a) Calculate the fraction and percent of ³⁷Cl. (b) Explain why the average molecular mass of CH₂Cl₂ is not itself a single peak in its mass spectrum; name the three isotope-combination masses that produce the cluster.
hints: Let y be the ³⁷Cl fraction and 1−y the ³⁵Cl fraction.
A mass spectrum records discrete isotope combinations, not a weighted mean.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 1.4 Calculate average atomic and molecular masses based on isotopic abundance

questions.answer: 34.969(1−y)+36.966y=35.45, so 1.997y=0.481 and y=0.241: about 24.1% ³⁷Cl and 75.9% ³⁵Cl. CH₂Cl₂ has discrete molecular-isotope masses 84 (³⁵Cl₂), 86 (³⁵Cl³⁷Cl), and 88 (³⁷Cl₂). Its average molecular mass is a weighted mean, so it is not one of those discrete molecular-ion masses/peaks.
rubric: Sets up and solves the weighted-average equation to about 0.241.
Reports approximately 24% ³⁷Cl.
Names 84, 86, and 88 as the discrete CH₂Cl₂ isotope masses.
Explains why a weighted average is not an MS peak.
questions.explanation: A periodic-table average mass summarizes a population; MS resolves individual isotope combinations.

questions.prompt: Use these average bond dissociation energies: H–H 436 kJ/mol, F–F 155 kJ/mol, H–F 565 kJ/mol. (a) Calculate Δ = BDEHF − √(BDEHH×BDEFF). (b) Use Δχ = 0.102√Δ to estimate the electronegativity difference. (c) Explain why breaking an H–F bond has positive ΔH but forming it has negative ΔH.
hints: Keep Δ in kJ/mol before applying the 0.102 relationship.
Bond breaking and bond forming have opposite energy directions.

sourceRefs.file: Courses/CHEM 042 - Chemistry in the Modern World/Midterm 1 - Master Study Guide.md
sourceRefs.heading: 1.8 Define bond dissociation energies and use them to evaluate bond strength

questions.answer: √(436×155)=√67580=260.0 kJ/mol. Δ=565−260=305 kJ/mol. Δχ=0.102√305=0.102(17.46)=1.78. Breaking H–F requires energy to overcome the attractive bond, so ΔH>0. Bond formation creates that attraction and releases energy, so ΔH<0.
rubric: Calculates the geometric mean near 260 and Δ near 305 kJ/mol.
Obtains Δχ about 1.78.
Correctly assigns positive ΔH to breaking and negative ΔH to forming with an energy explanation.
questions.explanation: BDE is defined for homolytic bond breaking in the gas phase.

Compare which candidate contains an O–H bond.

(b) Δx = γ(Δx′ + VΔt′) = (5⁄4)[15 c · hr + (⅗c)(4 hr)] = 87⁄4 c · hr.

(c) VΔx′ ⁄ c² is the relativity-of-simultaneity term: separated events in S′ affect the time interval assigned in S.

questions.explanation: Neither transformed term can be dropped because both Δt′ and Δx′ are nonzero.
